lessons.title: Affination and Melting of Raw Sugar
lessons.body: Raw sugar from a mill is covered in a film of molasses. Affination removes this film by mixing the raw sugar with a heavy syrup (about 70-75 Brix) in a magma mixer. The mixture is then spun in centrifugals to separate the syrup from the sugar crystals. In Africa, many refineries use batch centrifugals for this step. The syrup, called affination syrup, is recycled or sold as a byproduct. After affination, the sugar is melted with hot water or sweet water to form a liquor of 60-65 Brix. This melting step is done in a melter equipped with steam coils and agitation. The liquor is then screened to remove debris like bagasse, sand, and metal pieces. In small-scale operations in countries like Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa, a simple tank with a stirrer and steam injection can be used. The melted liquor is then pumped to clarification. Key parameters: affination syrup Brix should be 70-75, temperature around 60-70Â°C. Melting water temperature should be 80-90Â°C. The purity of the melted liquor should be at least 98%. This step is crucial because it reduces color and ash, making subsequent refining easier. Without proper affination, the final white sugar will have high color and may fail quality standards.

lessons.title: Clarification and Decolorization: Carbonatation and Phosphatation
lessons.body: After melting, the raw liquor still contains impurities like gums, waxes, and colorants. Clarification removes these. Two main methods are used: carbonatation and phosphatation. In carbonatation, lime (calcium hydroxide) is added to the liquor to raise pH to about 8.5-9.0. Then carbon dioxide gas is bubbled through, forming calcium carbonate precipitate. This precipitate traps impurities and color. The mixture is then filtered. Carbonatation is common in large refineries in South Africa and Egypt. In phosphatation, phosphoric acid is added, followed by lime to form calcium phosphate precipitate. This method is simpler and used in smaller plants. The pH is adjusted to about 7.5-8.0. After precipitation, a flocculant is added to help settle the precipitate. The clear liquor is then decolorized using activated carbon or bone char. In Africa, bone char is used in some refineries, but activated carbon is more common due to availability. The decolorization step reduces color from about 1000 ICUMSA to less than 100. Temperature during clarification is kept at 70-80Â°C. Proper control of pH and chemical dosage is critical. Over-liming can cause scaling, while under-liming leaves impurities. This step ensures the final sugar is bright and pure.

lessons.title: Filtration and Ion Exchange Resins
lessons.body: Filtration removes the precipitate formed during clarification. Common equipment includes plate-and-frame filter presses, rotary vacuum filters, and pressure leaf filters. In African refineries, plate-and-frame presses are often used because they are robust and easy to maintain. Filter aids like diatomaceous earth (DE) are used to improve filtration. The filtered liquor should be clear, with turbidity less than 5 NTU. After filtration, the liquor may still contain dissolved color and ions. Ion exchange resins are used for further decolorization and demineralization. Strong base anion resins remove color bodies, while cation resins remove metal ions like calcium and magnesium. In a typical setup, the liquor passes through a series of columns: first a cation resin (to remove cations), then an anion resin (to remove anions and color). The resins are regenerated with sodium chloride (for anion) and hydrochloric acid (for cation). In small-scale operations in Africa, ion exchange may be skipped if the sugar is for local markets with less strict color standards. However, for export-quality white sugar, ion exchange is essential. The resin beds must be backwashed regularly to prevent fouling. The flow rate should be controlled to ensure proper contact time. This step can reduce color to below 20 ICUMSA and ash to less than 0.01%.

lessons.title: Crystallization in Refining: White Sugar Production
lessons.body: Crystallization is the heart of white sugar production. The clarified and decolorized liquor is concentrated in evaporators to about 65-70 Brix, then further boiled in vacuum pans to form crystals. In refining, the process is done in multiple stages: first, a high-purity liquor is boiled to produce white sugar crystals. The vacuum pan is operated under vacuum to lower the boiling temperature to about 60-70Â°C, preventing color formation. Seed crystals are added to start crystallization. The pan is then fed with more liquor until the crystals reach the desired size (typically 0.4-0.6 mm). The mixture, called massecuite, is then dropped into crystallizers for cooling and further crystal growth. In Africa, many refineries use batch vacuum pans. The boiling time can be 2-4 hours. The purity of the mother liquor drops as sugar crystallizes. The massecuite is then sent to centrifugals. The first crop of crystals is the white sugar. The mother liquor (run-off) is reboiled to produce lower-grade sugars, which are recycled back to affination or sold as brown sugar. Key control points: vacuum level (about 600-650 mmHg), temperature, and supersaturation (1.1-1.3). Proper seeding and boiling ensure uniform crystal size and good yield.

lessons.title: Centrifugation and Drying of Refined Sugar
lessons.body: After crystallization, the massecuite is separated into crystals and mother liquor using centrifugals. In refining, high-speed batch centrifugals are used for white sugar. The centrifugal basket has a fine screen (0.06-0.08 mm openings) that retains crystals while allowing syrup to pass. The cycle includes loading, spinning, washing, and discharging. Washing is done with hot water (about 80-90Â°C) to remove the film of mother liquor from the crystals. The wash water is then spun off. The spinning time is typically 3-5 minutes. The sugar is then discharged and sent to dryers. Drying reduces moisture from about 1-2% to less than 0.05%. Common dryers are rotary drum dryers and fluidized bed dryers. In African refineries, rotary dryers are common. Hot air at 60-80Â°C is passed through the dryer. After drying, the sugar is cooled to below 30Â°C and then screened to remove lumps and fines. The final product is stored in silos or bags. Proper centrifugation and drying are critical for sugar quality: moisture above 0.05% can cause caking, and residual syrup can cause color development. The centrifugals must be well maintained to avoid screen damage, which can lead to sugar loss.

lessons.title: Quality Parameters for Refined Sugar
lessons.body: Refined sugar must meet strict quality standards. Key parameters include: color (ICUMSA), moisture, ash, invert sugar, and particle size. For white sugar, ICUMSA color should be less than 45 (often 20-30 for premium grade). Moisture should be below 0.05%. Ash content should be less than 0.01%. Invert sugar should be less than 0.04% to prevent deterioration. Particle size distribution: typically 0.3-0.8 mm, with uniform size for even packaging. In Africa, standards vary by country. For example, Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) requires ICUMSA color max 100 for white sugar, while South Africa (SABS) requires max 50. Export to the EU requires ICUMSA less than 45. Other tests include: turbidity, insoluble matter, and heavy metals (lead, arsenic) which must be below 1 ppm. Microbiological tests for yeast, mould, and bacteria are also done. To achieve these, every step from affination to drying must be controlled. Regular sampling and testing in a laboratory are essential. Small refineries can use simple tests like a refractometer for Brix and a colorimeter for ICUMSA. Maintaining quality ensures market access and premium prices. Training staff on hygiene and equipment cleaning is also vital to prevent contamination.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Refining of Raw Sugar

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons of the Refining of Raw Sugar module into a single working document for African sugar processors, quality managers, and operations teams. It is written for people who need to make decisions â on equipment, on consumables, on market compliance â not just understand theory. Use it alongside the lesson modules as a bench-side guide, a training aid, and a planning tool.

Africa produces roughly 10â12 million tonnes of sugar annually, with major producers including Egypt, South Africa, Sudan, Eswatini, Mauritius, Kenya, and Zambia. Most of this is plantation white or raw sugar, but a growing share is refined white sugar for direct human consumption, beverages, confectionery, and export. Refining margins are thin; the difference between a profitable refinery and a struggling one is usually yield recovery, energy efficiency, and consistent quality compliance. This reference focuses on those three levers.

Process Flow at a Glance

Data Table 1: Typical Operating Parameters by Process Stage

Stage Key Parameter Typical Range Business Impact if Off-Spec

Melting Melt liquor Â°Brix / pH 65â70 Â°Brix; pH 7.0â7.5 Off-pH causes inversion, sucrose loss (revenue loss), scale formation
Carbonatation Lime dose / COâ / pH 0.5â1.0% CaO on solids; pH 10.5â11.5 first sat. Under-dosing â poor colour removal; over-dosing â molasses loss in filter cake
Phosphatation Phosphoric acid dose / pH 0.03â0.06% PâOâ on solids; pH 7.0â7.5 Wrong floc â slow filtration, high turbidity, rework
Ion exchange Resin bed volume, flow rate 2â4 BV/h; regeneration every 12â24 h Breakthrough â colour spike, off-spec white sugar, rejected export consignment
Crystallization Strike temperature / supersaturation 65â75 Â°C; S = 1.1â1.3 Fines or conglomerates â poor centrifugal performance, yield loss
Centrifugation Cycle time / wash water 2â4 min batch; wash 5â10% on massecuite Excess wash â molasses dilution, energy cost; too little â high colour
Drying Outlet moisture / temperature <0.04% moisture; 40â60 Â°C outlet Moisture >0.05% â caking, microbial risk, retail complaints

Sources: Chou (2000), Handbook of Sugar Refining; MeadeâChen Cane Sugar Handbook (12th ed.); ICUMSA Method GS1/3-7; Sugar Industry Research Institute (SIRI) operational bulletins, Mauritius.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CRITICAL CONTROL POINTS

Lime and COâ handling: Carbonatation uses hydrated lime (Ca(OH)â) â a strong alkali causing severe eye and skin burns. COâ gas is an asphyxiant in confined spaces. Always use closed dosing systems, personal protective equipment (goggles, face shield, chemical gloves, apron), and COâ monitors in the saturator area.
Ion exchange regeneration: Resin regeneration uses hydrochloric acid (HCl) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH) â highly corrosive. Never mix acid and caustic streams. Provide emergency eyewash and deluge showers within 10 seconds' reach, and store acids and bases in separate bunded areas.
Centrifugal machines: Never open a basket centrifuge before full deceleration â high-speed ejection of hot massecuite causes fatal scalding. Interlock the lid with the drive.
Rotary dryers: Sugar dust is combustible. Maintain bonding and grounding of all metal parts, use explosion-vented dryers, and keep ignition sources away from the drying zone. Dust explosion is a real risk in African refineries with older equipment.

Quick Reference Checklist â Daily Refinery Operations

  1. Affination syrup: Verify Â°Brix (70â75) and temperature (45â55 Â°C) at start of shift. Check that the wash syrup is being recycled to the melt, not dumped.
  2. Melt pH and Â°Brix: Confirm 65â70 Â°Brix and pH 7.0â7.5 before clarification. Log every adjustment â pH drift is the earliest sign of process trouble.
  3. Lime and COâ dosing: Check dosing pumps calibrated weekly. Confirm first carbonatation pH 10.5â11.5 and second carbonatation pH 8.0â8.5.
  4. Filter performance: Monitor filter cake moisture and clarity of filtrate. A sudden drop in throughput means floc failure or cloth blinding.
  5. Ion exchange: Track colour of exit liquor hourly. Regenerate on schedule â do not stretch cycles to save chemicals; breakthrough cost is far higher than regeneration cost.
  6. Crystallization: Verify supersaturation via refractometer or boiling point elevation. Check crystal size distribution every strike. Adjust seed and cooling curve.
  7. Centrifugals: Confirm wash water flow and cycle time. Inspect screens for tears at every shift change. Log sugar colour after each batch.
  8. Drying and packing: Check outlet moisture (<0.04%) and temperature (<60 Â°C). Verify metal detector and magnet function before packing. Record lot number and ICUMSA colour for traceability.

Business-First Notes for African Refineries

Refining economics in Africa are dominated by three cost drivers: energy (boilers, evaporators, dryers), chemicals (lime, phosphoric acid, resins, filter aids), and sucrose recovery (molasses loss, undetermined losses). A 0.5% improvement in recovery on a 500 t/day refinery is worth roughly 900 tonnes of sugar per year â at USD 400â500/tonne, that is USD 360,000â450,000 in additional revenue. Small process discipline gains translate directly into cash.

Export markets matter. EU and UK buyers require ICUMSA 45 with full traceability, SOâ limits, and often sustainability certification (Bonsucro, Fairtrade, or Rainforest Alliance). Regional markets (ECOWAS, COMESA, SADC) accept ICUMSA 100â150 and are less demanding on documentation, but price is lower. A refinery that can switch grades on the same line without long changeover times has a strategic advantage.

Power reliability is a recurring constraint. Where grid supply is unstable, invest in a standby generator sized for the centrifugal and drying sections â a stoppage during crystallization can ruin an entire strike and cost hours of rework.

Further Reading â Free Official Resources

  • ICUMSA â International Commission for Uniform Methods of Sugar Analysis (official methods, colour, polarization)
  • FAOSTAT â Sugar Crops and Sugar Production Data (African production and trade statistics)
  • FAO â Small-Scale Sugar Processing Manual (practical guidance for developing-country processors)
  • Codex Alimentarius â Standard for Sugars (CODEX STAN 212-1999) (international quality and labelling standards)
  • ISO 2468 / ISO 2469 â Sugar Refractometry and Colour Measurement (instrument calibration references)

Prepared for Rise Africa Skills â Sugar Processing Course, Module: Refining of Raw Sugar. Practical Reference lesson. Version 1.0.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of affination in sugar refining?
options: A) To remove molasses film from raw sugar crystals
quiz.explanation: Affination removes the molasses coating on raw sugar crystals by mixing with syrup and centrifuging.

quiz.q: What is the typical Brix of affination syrup?
quiz.explanation: Affination syrup is typically 70-75 Brix to effectively remove molasses.

quiz.q: After affination, raw sugar is melted to form a liquor of what Brix?
quiz.explanation: Melted liquor is usually 60-65 Brix for further processing.

quiz.q: Which chemical is added in carbonatation to raise pH?
quiz.explanation: Lime is added to raise pH to about 8.5-9.0 in carbonatation.

quiz.q: What gas is bubbled through in carbonatation?
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide forms calcium carbonate precipitate with lime.

quiz.q: In phosphatation, what acid is added?
quiz.explanation: Phosphoric acid is used in phosphatation to form calcium phosphate precipitate.

quiz.q: What is the typical pH range for phosphatation?
quiz.explanation: Phosphatation is carried out at pH 7.5-8.0 for optimal precipitation.

quiz.q: Which decolorizing agent is commonly used in African refineries?
quiz.explanation: Activated carbon is more common due to availability, though bone char is also used.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of filtration after clarification?
quiz.explanation: Filtration removes the precipitate formed during clarification.

quiz.q: Which filter aid is commonly used in sugar refining?
quiz.explanation: Diatomaceous earth is used to improve filtration efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the typical turbidity of filtered liquor?
quiz.explanation: Filtered liquor should be clear with turbidity less than 5 NTU.

quiz.q: Which resin removes color bodies?
quiz.explanation: Strong base anion resins remove color bodies and anions.

quiz.q: How are anion resins regenerated?
quiz.explanation: Anion resins are regenerated with sodium chloride (brine).

quiz.q: What is the typical color reduction achieved by ion exchange?
quiz.explanation: Ion exchange can reduce color to below 20 ICUMSA.

quiz.q: In crystallization, what is the typical vacuum level in the pan?
quiz.explanation: Vacuum pans operate at about 600-650 mmHg to lower boiling temperature.

quiz.q: What is the typical crystal size for white sugar?
quiz.explanation: White sugar crystals are typically 0.4-0.6 mm.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of seeding in crystallization?
quiz.explanation: Seed crystals provide nuclei for crystal growth.

quiz.q: What is massecuite?
options: A) Mixture of crystals and mother liquor
quiz.explanation: Massecuite is the mixture of sugar crystals and mother liquor from the vacuum pan.

quiz.q: In centrifugation, what is the purpose of washing?
options: A) To remove mother liquor film
quiz.explanation: Washing with hot water removes the film of mother liquor from crystals.

quiz.q: What is the typical spinning time in batch centrifugals?
quiz.explanation: Spinning time is typically 3-5 minutes to separate crystals and syrup.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content after drying?
quiz.explanation: Drying reduces moisture to below 0.05% to prevent caking.

quiz.q: Which dryer is common in African refineries?
quiz.explanation: Rotary drum dryers are commonly used due to their robustness.

quiz.q: What is the typical hot air temperature in a rotary dryer?
quiz.explanation: Hot air at 60-80Â°C is used to dry sugar without caramelization.

quiz.q: What is the maximum ICUMSA color for premium white sugar?
quiz.explanation: Premium white sugar typically has ICUMSA color less than 45.

quiz.q: What is the typical ash content of refined white sugar?
quiz.explanation: Refined white sugar should have ash content below 0.01%.

quiz.q: Why is invert sugar content important?
quiz.explanation: High invert sugar can lead to deterioration and quality loss.

quiz.q: Which organization sets sugar standards in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) sets sugar quality standards in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is the maximum heavy metal content (lead, arsenic) in refined sugar?
quiz.explanation: Heavy metals like lead and arsenic must be below 1 ppm.

quiz.q: What simple test can be used to measure Brix in a small refinery?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer is a simple tool for measuring Brix.

quiz.q: Why is staff training on hygiene important?
quiz.explanation: Proper hygiene prevents microbial and physical contamination of sugar.
